name: Lofexidine (Lucemyra)
summary: Non-opioid, alpha-2 adrenergic medication used to take the edge off opioid withdrawal symptoms during detox. Helps calm the body's stress response but can lower blood pressure and heart rate.
description: Lucemyra (lofexidine) is used short-term to reduce opioid withdrawal symptoms so people can stop opioids abruptly under medical supervision. It does not treat opioid use disorder by itself and it does not prevent relapse. Common effects include dizziness, low blood pressure, slow heart rate, dry mouth, and feeling sedated—plus insomnia is still very common during withdrawal. Because it can affect heart rhythm (QT prolongation), it needs extra caution in higher-risk patients and with certain meds.
patient_summary: Lucemyra is a short-term, non-opioid med that helps reduce opioid withdrawal symptoms during detox. It doesn't treat opioid use disorder or protect against relapse. It can cause low blood pressure, slow heart rate, dizziness, and sedation, and it can affect QT interval in some people—so monitoring matters, especially if you have heart, liver, or kidney issues or take other QT-prolonging meds.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved to reduce opioid withdrawal symptoms to support abrupt opioid discontinuation. It's a withdrawal-symptom tool, not a full opioid use disorder treatment.

May be used inside a comprehensive opioid use disorder plan, but it does not treat OUD by itself and does not prevent relapse. MOUD (buprenorphine or methadone) remains first-line for OUD when appropriate.

contraindications: There are no contraindications listed in the manufacturer's labeling.

efficacy_response.patient_text: Lucemyra isn't about being 'cured'—it’s about making withdrawal more tolerable by dialing down the body's fight-or-flight surge. Many people still feel uncomfortable, but symptoms like sweating, chills, restlessness, and racing heart can be less intense.

pharmacokinetics.half_life: 11 to 13 hours after first dose; 17 to 22 hours at steady state
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: First-pass metabolism; primarily hepatic via CYP2D6, with contributions from CYP1A2 and CYP2C19
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be administered with or without food

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Lucemyra is used to reduce opioid withdrawal symptoms during detox so people can stop opioids abruptly under medical supervision. It does not treat opioid use disorder by itself, and it does not protect you from relapse—it's a symptom-relief tool inside a bigger treatment plan.
items: {link:condition:opioid-withdrawal:Opioid Withdrawal}: Helps reduce the intensity of withdrawal symptoms during the first days after stopping opioids
Withdrawal support during detox: Often used during the peak withdrawal window (usually the first week) as part of a structured program

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s withdrawal is different, but these are the patterns people describe with Lucemyra:

quotes: It didn’t erase withdrawal, but it turned the volume down on the panic-y, crawling-out-of-my-skin feeling.
My heart wasn’t pounding as hard and I wasn’t sweating through everything.
It made the physical surge feel less violent, like my body wasn’t screaming as much.
Standing up too fast was a mistake—felt woozy and had to sit down.
I felt kind of faint sometimes, like my blood pressure was running low.
I learned quickly: hydrate, move slow, and don’t try to be a hero.
items.note: Dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are common. Slow position changes help.

quotes: I felt tired and heavy, but my sleep was still trash.
It made me drowsy in the day… and then somehow I still had insomnia at night.
Calm body, restless brain. Withdrawal is weird.
items.note: Insomnia is very common during withdrawal even when daytime sedation happens.

quotes: If I pushed the next dose too late, I could feel the symptoms creep back in.
Every 5-6 hours felt real—when I slipped, withdrawal reminded me fast.
The schedule mattered more than I expected.
items.note: It’s typically dosed four times daily during peak withdrawal symptoms.

quotes: I didn’t realize how sensitive I’d be—going back to my old dose could’ve killed me.
They warned me: don’t relapse at your previous amount. Your tolerance isn’t what you think it is.
The scariest part was learning how easy overdose becomes after detox.
items.note: After withdrawal treatment, people may respond to lower opioid doses than before—overdose risk rises if relapse occurs.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Lucemyra isn’t an instant switch-off like a sedative. It works by calming the body’s overactive sympathetic “alarm system,” so the change is often felt as a gradual reduction in the physical surge of withdrawal.
key_points: Peak levels: ~3 to 5 hours after a dose
Typical use window: Most commonly during peak withdrawal (often the first 5 to 7 days after last opioid use), with treatment up to 14 days if needed
Half-life: ~11 to 13 hours after the first dose; ~17 to 22 hours at steady state
Dosing rhythm: Often taken every 5 to 6 hours during the day to keep symptoms steadier

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Lucemyra is best thought of as a “withdrawal symptom dampener.” It can reduce the intensity of symptoms driven by norepinephrine (sweats, chills, restlessness, agitation), but it won’t necessarily fix insomnia, cravings, or the emotional spiral on its own. It works best when it’s part of a full withdrawal and opioid use disorder plan.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Lucemyra is not opioid use disorder treatment. After detox, relapse at your old dose can be fatal.
other: Accidental opioid overdose risk after treatment: After withdrawal management, tolerance can drop fast. People may respond to much lower opioid doses than they used before, increasing overdose risk if relapse occurs.
Cardiovascular effects: Can cause low blood pressure, slow heart rate, orthostatic hypotension, and fainting. Higher risk in people with significant heart disease or baseline bradycardia.
CNS depression: Can cause sedation and slowed reaction time—driving and machinery can be unsafe.
QT prolongation risk: Can prolong QT interval; avoid in congenital long QT syndrome and use extra caution in higher-risk patients or with QT-prolonging meds.
Do not stop abruptly: Sudden discontinuation can cause a rebound spike in blood pressure plus withdrawal-like symptoms (anxiety, chills, diarrhea, sweating, insomnia, pain).
patient_counseling: This medication helps withdrawal symptoms, but it does not treat opioid use disorder. Long-term recovery usually needs meds like buprenorphine or methadone, plus therapy/support.
Move slowly from lying/sitting to standing. Dizziness and fainting can happen—especially early on.
Avoid driving or risky tasks until you know how sedating it is for you.
Tell your clinician if you have heart disease, a history of fainting, or you take QT-prolonging meds.
Do not stop Lucemyra suddenly. If you’re finishing the course, taper over a few days as directed.
Overdose warning: If you return to opioids after detox, your old dose can be deadly. Treat relapse as a medical emergency risk, not a moral failure.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: low blood pressure, slow heart rate, dizziness, sedation, dry mouth, and insomnia (yes—insomnia can still be extremely common during withdrawal).
plain_language_list: Low blood pressure (including when standing up) and feeling faint

common.patient_note: Your pulse can run lower than usual. If you feel faint, weak, or like you might pass out—especially with chest symptoms—contact your clinician right away.
Low blood pressure can feel like fatigue, weakness, or lightheadedness. Hydration and slow position changes help, but dose adjustments may be needed if it’s clinically significant.
This is the classic “stand up and the room tilts” side effect. It’s common. Go slow, hold onto something, and sit back down if you get dizzy.
Often overlaps with low blood pressure. Avoid sudden movements and be careful on stairs.
Expect some sedation. It can be helpful for agitation, but it can also impair coordination and reaction time.
Withdrawal insomnia can be brutal, and Lucemyra doesn’t necessarily fix it. Sometimes it helps the physical agitation but sleep still lags behind.
Sugar-free gum, hydration, and oral care help. Dry mouth can worsen dental issues over time.

serious: Syncope (fainting): can happen with low blood pressure or bradycardia—especially with dehydration or standing quickly.
QT prolongation and torsades de pointes (rare but serious): higher risk in at-risk patients, electrolyte abnormalities, or when combined with QT-prolonging medications.
Clinically significant hypotension/bradycardia: may require dose reduction or interruption of therapy.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Lucemyra has meaningful interaction risk. The two big buckets are (1) meds that further lower blood pressure/heart rate and (2) meds that increase QT prolongation risk. It’s also a CYP2D6 substrate, so metabolism differences and CYP2D6-related interactions can matter.

items.with: QT-prolonging medications (multiple classes: some antipsychotics, some antidepressants, some antibiotics, antiarrhythmics)
items.risk: Additive QT prolongation increases risk of dangerous arrhythmias, especially in people with bradycardia, heart failure, electrolyte problems, or liver/kidney impairment.
items.action: Avoid when possible. If combined is necessary, correct electrolytes first and monitor ECG in at-risk patients.

items.with: Other blood pressure or heart rate lowering agents (antihypertensives, some antiarrhythmics)
items.action: Use caution. Monitor vitals and consider dose reductions or spacing adjustments.

items.with: CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds, muscle relaxants)
items.risk: More sedation, slowed reaction time, falls, impaired judgment.
items.action: Use caution and avoid stacking sedatives whenever possible, especially during detox when dehydration and instability are common.

items.with: CYP2D6 inhibitors or CYP2D6 poor metabolizer status
items.risk: Higher exposure may increase orthostasis, bradycardia, and QT effects.
items.action: Monitor closely for dizziness, fainting, and low heart rate; dose adjustments may be needed.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Don’t stop Lucemyra abruptly. Stopping suddenly can cause a rebound spike in blood pressure and a cluster of withdrawal-like symptoms (anxiety, chills, diarrhea, sweating, insomnia, pain). The usual move is a short taper over a few days.
key_points: Typical discontinuation: Taper over 2 to 4 days to reduce rebound symptoms.
Example taper strategy: Reduce by 0.18 mg per dose every 1 to 2 days.
If rebound symptoms show up (blood pressure surge, anxiety, sweats, chills, diarrhea, insomnia): slow the taper and reassess.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Lucemyra is typically taken four times daily during peak opioid withdrawal symptoms, then adjusted based on how you’re tolerating it and how withdrawal is evolving. The biggest limiter is blood pressure and heart rate—if you get symptomatic hypotension or bradycardia, dosing often needs to be reduced or paused.

adult.opioid_withdrawal_initial: 0.54 mg PO QID (every 5 to 6 hours) during peak withdrawal symptoms (generally first 5 to 7 days after last opioid use)
adult.opioid_withdrawal_titration: Adjust based on tolerability and withdrawal symptoms; lower doses may be appropriate as symptoms wane; may continue up to 14 days if needed
adult.opioid_withdrawal_max: 0.72 mg per dose OR 2.88 mg/day maximum total
adult.discontinuation_taper: Taper over 2 to 4 days (example: reduce by 0.18 mg per dose every 1 to 2 days)
adult.renal_adjustment: eGFR 30 to 89.9 mL/min/1.73 m2: 0.36 mg PO QID; eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2: 0.18 mg PO QID; ESRD/hemodialysis: 0.18 mg PO QID (minimally dialyzable; administer without regard to dialysis timing)
adult.hepatic_adjustment: Child-Pugh A: no adjustment; Child-Pugh B: 0.36 mg PO QID; Child-Pugh C: 0.18 mg PO QID
adult.older_adults: Refer to adult dosing; use with caution; consider lower doses

sections.simple_explanation: Lucemyra is scheduled (not PRN) during the worst withdrawal window. The goal is to blunt the body’s overactive stress response without pushing blood pressure or heart rate too low. As withdrawal fades, doses often step down, then taper off over a few days.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding data are limited. Also, kidney and liver function matter because QT risk and drug exposure can increase when clearance is reduced. Older adults may be more sensitive to low blood pressure and falls.
sections.pregnancy: Information related to the use of lofexidine in pregnancy is limited. Abrupt discontinuation of opioid therapy in dependent patients is generally not recommended during pregnancy.
sections.lactation: It is not known if lofexidine is present in breast milk. Lofexidine should be used with caution in breastfeeding patients; the decision to breastfeed during therapy should consider the risk of infant exposure, the benefits of breastfeeding to the infant, and benefits of treatment to the mother.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing; use with caution; consider lower doses based on blood pressure, heart rate, fall risk, and overall tolerability.
sections.hepatic: Prolongation of the QTc interval may be more pronounced in patients with severe hepatic impairment. Use caution in hepatic impairment and follow recommended dose reductions in moderate and severe impairment.
sections.renal: Prolongation of the QTc interval may be more pronounced in patients with severe renal impairment. Use caution in renal impairment and follow recommended dose reductions; avoid use in chronic renal failure.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Blood pressure and heart rate (baseline and during therapy), including orthostatic vitals if dizziness/faintness is present
Opioid withdrawal symptom severity over time to guide dose adjustments
Sedation and functional impairment (falls risk, driving safety, slowed reaction time)
Electrolytes and ECG at baseline in at-risk populations (eg, heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, congenital long QT risk, or concomitant QT-prolonging medications)
Symptoms of clinically significant bradycardia/hypotension (fainting, near-syncope, severe weakness) that may require dose reduction or interruption of therapy
Relapse and overdose risk counseling: reinforce that post-detox opioid tolerance is lower and old doses can be fatal

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: In the U.S., lofexidine is available as oral tablets. The dosing is built around 0.18 mg tablets, which makes step-down tapers and dose reductions straightforward.
items: Tablet, oral (Lucemyra): 0.18 mg (contains FD&C Yellow #6 / Sunset Yellow)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Lucemyra is a central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. In plain terms: it lowers norepinephrine release and calms the sympathetic nervous system—the part of your body that goes full fight-or-flight during opioid withdrawal. By reducing that surge, it can lessen symptoms like sweats, chills, restlessness, agitation, and the pounding “wired” feeling.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Lucemyra fits into withdrawal management, not long-term opioid use disorder treatment. It can help people get through detox more safely and comfortably, but it does not treat addiction on its own and does not reduce relapse risk the way medications for opioid use disorder (like buprenorphine or methadone) do. Clinically, it’s used when someone is doing an abrupt opioid stop and needs non-opioid symptom support, while keeping a sharp eye on blood pressure, heart rate, and QT risk—especially in people with kidney or liver impairment.

seo.title: Lofexidine (Lucemyra): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Detox Safety
seo.description: Lucemyra (lofexidine) for opioid withdrawal: what it helps, dosing (0.54 mg QID; max 2.88 mg/day), common side effects (low BP, slow HR, dizziness, sedation), QT warning, interactions, and how to taper off safely.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Lucemyra (lofexidine) is used short-term to reduce opioid withdrawal symptoms during detox so someone can stop opioids abruptly under medical supervision. It’s not a treatment for opioid use disorder by itself, and it doesn’t prevent relapse.

No. Lucemyra helps withdrawal symptoms, but it does not treat opioid use disorder or reduce relapse risk on its own. Long-term treatment usually involves medications like buprenorphine or methadone (plus therapy and support).

faqs.q: What symptoms does Lucemyra help the most?
faqs.a: It mainly targets the body’s overactive fight-or-flight symptoms—things like sweating, chills, restlessness, agitation, and a racing heart. It may not fix insomnia or cravings by itself, and those often need additional support.

faqs.q: How is Lucemyra dosed for opioid withdrawal?
faqs.a: A common adult starting schedule is 0.54 mg by mouth four times daily (about every 5 to 6 hours) during peak withdrawal symptoms. Doses are adjusted based on tolerability and symptoms, with a maximum of 0.72 mg per dose or 2.88 mg/day total. Treatment can continue up to 14 days if needed.

faqs.q: Why do people feel dizzy or faint on Lucemyra?
faqs.a: Lucemyra can lower blood pressure and slow heart rate. That can cause dizziness, especially when standing up (orthostatic hypotension). Hydration and slow position changes help, but if symptoms are significant, dosing may need to be reduced or paused.

faqs.q: Can Lucemyra affect the heart rhythm?
faqs.a: Yes, it can prolong the QT interval in some people. Risk is higher in congenital long QT syndrome and in people with bradycardia, heart failure, electrolyte abnormalities, and severe liver or kidney impairment—or when combined with QT-prolonging medications. ECG monitoring may be recommended in higher-risk cases.

faqs.q: Can I stop Lucemyra suddenly when detox is over?
faqs.a: Don’t stop it abruptly. Stopping suddenly can cause rebound high blood pressure and symptoms like anxiety, chills, diarrhea, sweating, insomnia, and pain. The usual approach is tapering the dose over 2 to 4 days (for example, reducing by 0.18 mg per dose every 1 to 2 days).

faqs.q: What’s the biggest safety warning after finishing Lucemyra?
faqs.a: Overdose risk if relapse happens. After detox, your opioid tolerance can be much lower than you remember. Going back to your old dose can be life-threatening. If relapse risk is high, talk with your clinician about medications for opioid use disorder and overdose prevention (like naloxone).

faqs.q: Can Lucemyra be used in kidney or liver impairment?
faqs.a: Yes, but doses are reduced as kidney or liver function declines. In moderate renal impairment (eGFR 30–89.9), a common dose is 0.36 mg four times daily; in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) it’s often 0.18 mg four times daily; and in ESRD/hemodialysis it’s often 0.18 mg four times daily. For hepatic impairment: Child-Pugh A usually needs no adjustment; Child-Pugh B is often 0.36 mg four times daily; Child-Pugh C is often 0.18 mg four times daily.

faqs.q: Is Lucemyra safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Pregnancy data are limited, and abrupt opioid discontinuation during pregnancy is generally not recommended in opioid-dependent patients. It’s also not known whether lofexidine is present in breast milk. If lofexidine is being considered in pregnancy or breastfeeding, it should be a specialized, high-caution decision with a clear risk/benefit discussion and a comprehensive treatment plan.
